problem: Existing VLN instruction generators (Speaker-Follower, EnvDrop) used for data augmentation were never evaluated with human wayfinders, and the automatic text metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, CIDEr) used to develop them were never validated against human wayfinding outcomes.
motivation: Better grounded instruction generation could improve wayfinding agents, but this needs reliable evaluation. The authors observe that metrics validated only on captioning may be uninformative for grounded, sequenced navigation instructions. They therefore run human wayfinding studies and propose a reference-free instruction-trajectory compatibility model.
key_idea: Benchmark instruction generators with human wayfinders, show that standard n-gram metrics fail to track human outcomes, and train a dual-encoder instruction-trajectory compatibility model (contrastive + focal loss, hard negatives from instruction and path perturbations) as a reference-free metric.
insight: Contrastive in-batch losses add 9-10% AUC over CE/focal alone (rows 2-3 vs 4-6). Hard negatives need both instruction and path perturbations: using only one type, or none, gives ~69-70.5 val AUC vs 73.5 for both (rows 9, 13, 17 vs 8), and each perturbation type only detects its own failure mode. Metrics that score generators highly (BLEU, CIDEr) rate human instructions poorly (appendix table), so n-gram overlap is not grounding. Only SPICE tracks human performance at system level, and model-based scores work at instance level.
method: Human wayfinding benchmark: 3 human wayfinders per instruction in PanGEA on R2R val-seen (340 paths) and val-unseen (783); instructions from Speaker-Follower, EnvDrop, Crafty (template), human, and three perturbed human variants; 11,886 attempts, 37 annotators; metrics NE, SR, SPL, SDTW, Likert quality, visual search cost, time.
Crafty: template-based generator using an IDF-based Appraiser, Walker for motions, HMM Observer selecting landmark objects from ground-truth Matterport3D annotations, and a Talker with templates.

Instruction perturbations: Direction Swap, Entity Swap, Phrase Swap (remove/duplicate/shuffle sub-sentences) built with Google Cloud NLP parsing, used both as human-eval conditions and as hard negatives.

Dual-encoder compatibility model: BERT-embedding BiLSTM instruction encoder and a 2-layer LSTM over panoramas (36 views with attention, prev/next direction features, CNN + sin/cos angle features); score = cosine similarity of the final states.

Hard negative mining: trajectory perturbations (Random Walk, Path Reversal, Viewpoint Swap) plus instruction perturbations, sampled 2:1:1 for GT:instruction:trajectory; positives expanded to 110,601 pairs by round-trip back-translation through 10 languages with a BLEU filter of [0.25, 0.7]. The model is not trained on generator outputs.
Loss: in-batch contrastive loss over rows and columns of the N×N similarity matrix (learned temperature, perturbed diagonal entries skipped) + β·(focal loss γ=2 or CE) on sigmoid(aS+b), β=1.

Meta-evaluation: Kendall's τ at system level and instance level against human SR/SPL/NE/Quality, compared with BLEU/CIDEr/METEOR/ROUGE/SPICE, BERTScore, and VLN-agent SPL/SDTW scores; also AUC classification and data-augmentation filtering.

setting.backbone: Dual-encoder BERT + BiLSTM instruction encoder / 2-layer LSTM trajectory encoder (trained on R2R); VALAN VLN agent (Wang et al. 2018 style) for the augmentation experiment
setting.training_data: R2R train (~14k positive instruction-trajectory pairs, 4675 trajectories) expanded to 110,601 positives via back-translation, plus random and perturbation negatives; no generator outputs
setting.observation: Panoramic RGB image features (36 views) with heading/elevation angles along a trajectory, plus instruction text
setting.action_space: Not applicable (evaluation model); human wayfinders use the Matterport3D navigation graph
setting.privileged: Crafty baseline uses ground-truth object annotations; the compatibility model needs the candidate trajectory; reference-based metrics use the 3 R2R reference instructions

numbers.eval_set_note: 1700 instructions (78% high quality) from R2R human + Speaker-Follower + EnvDrop; high quality = 2 of 3 human wayfinders reached the goal
numbers.method: Contrastive + Focal + Paraphrase + BERT Embed. (row 8, path+instruction perturbations)
numbers.extra: model selected on val-unseen (3915 instructions); reports AUC
numbers.evidence: Table 2 row 8: Validation (val_unseen) 73.5, Test (val_seen) 73.7; prior work (Huang et al. 2019) row 1 gets 52.3

numbers.eval_set_note: 3915 instructions (75% high quality); used as validation
human wayfinding of the 783 trajectories, 3 wayfinders each; this benchmarks the existing generator EnvDrop, not the paper's own method (no own navigation agent)
numbers.extra: instructions from the authors of EnvDrop; only the instruction-generator benchmarking; not a proposed method

numbers_note: No proposed navigation agent; the paper is an evaluation study. Main results are AUC (Table 2) and Kendall's τ correlations (Table 3, given as 90% CIs). Instance-level compatibility τ vs Quality on all instructions is (0.19, 0.23) and on model-generated instructions is (0.18, 0.23). Data-augmentation results are only in a figure (model-ranked fractions beat random ones).
results: Human wayfinders show Speaker-Follower (SR 42.3 val-seen) and EnvDrop (SR 47.7 val-seen) are on par with or only slightly better than the template-based Crafty (43.6), and far worse than human instructions (75.1); they are even worse than adversarially perturbed human instructions (Phrase Swap 62.6). The compatibility model reaches 73.7 test AUC versus 52.3 for Huang et al. 2019, and matches the best instance-level correlation with human outcomes without references. SPICE is the only text metric correlating at system level.
limitations: Model-based metrics (compatibility, VLN agents, BERTScore) fail to rank out-of-domain systems (Crafty, perturbed, other annotators) at system level, with wide confidence intervals; only 9 systems (4 model-generated) are available.
The compatibility model is trained on R2R only, with modest absolute AUC (~74%), and has not been tested with transfer learning or used yet as a reward or generator.
Human evaluation covers English R2R, with human instructions collected only for val-seen and a small annotator pool of 37.
builds_on: Huang et al. 2019 (Transferable Representation Learning in VLN)
